title: Relationship with Previous Objectives
excerpt: There is a striking theoretical convergence between empowerment and expected free energy (EFE) minimization. While EFE minimizes the divergence between predicted and preferred outcomes, empowerment maximizes the channel capacity of the agent’s actuation. Howev
html:
There is a striking theoretical convergence between empowerment and expected free energy (EFE) minimization. While EFE minimizes the divergence between predicted and preferred outcomes, empowerment maximizes the channel capacity of the agent’s actuation. However, inspection of the decomposition reveals that empowerment is effectively a limit case of EFE minimization under specific priors. The conditional entropy term in empowerment, −H(St+k|st,At:t+k)-H(S_{t+k}|s_t,A_{t:t+k}), is analagous to the ambiguity term in EFE: both metrics drive the agent to minimize noise in the action-outcome mapping, penalizing policies where the consequences of control signals are uncertain. The divergence arises in the second term: empowerment explicitly maximizes the entropy of reachable states (H(St+k|st)H(S_{t+k}|s_t)), whereas EFE constrains outcomes to match a phenotypic prior P(oτ)P(o_\tau) (and when that distribution is sharp, it effectively favors low-entropy, "stasis-like" outcomes). This tension is resolved by recognizing that for a biological agent, the "preferred prior" P(oτ)P(o_\tau) is not a point-mass on a single stasis state, but a broad distribution over a viable phase space. Under a sufficiently flat prior over survival-compatible states, minimizing EFE requires the agent to "fill" the available state space (maximizing entropy within the viable set) to avoid overfitting to a specific, potentially fragile niche. This leads us to the idea of intrinsic motivation as constrained entropy maximization 1. Thus, empowerment can be viewed as the pure exploration / option value component of EFE: it is the objective function that dominates in proportion to how "flat" external reward signals (i.e risk) are, driving the agent to seize the "high ground" of the causal landscape where the agent can realize many distinct futures reliably.

The convergence of expected free energy, compression progress, and empowerment reveals that each framework captures a distinct but complementary facet of adaptive behavior–and that the brain’s apparent "objective function" is best understood as the dynamic arbitration among all three. EFE provides the overarching decision-theoretic scaffold: it specifies how to select policies that satisfy homeostatic and learned preferences (the risk term) while reducing state-level uncertainty (the ambiguity term), yielding a principled account of why organisms both exploit and sample even when sampling has no immediate reward 2, 3. However, EFE’s ambiguity term operates within a relatively fixed generative model–it rewards visiting diagnostic states but does not directly incentivize improving the model’s parameters. This is precisely what compression progress supplies: a learning-level objective that assigns intrinsic value to experiences that shrink description length, ensuring the generative model continually refines its structure and not just its state estimates. Meanwhile, empowerment captures something neither EFE nor compression directly addresses: the option value of a state independent of any currently active goal. An agent minimizing EFE with sharp preferences might converge on a narrow behavioral repertoire that satisfies current priors but leaves it vulnerable to distributional shift; an agent maximizing compression might obsessively model domains with no practical relevance. Empowerment provides a corrective prior toward states that preserve future flexibility–effectively a "strategic reserve" of controllable futures that hedges against model misspecification and goal change. Essentially, all three objectives are useful precisely because human behavior is a mixture of (1) constraint satisfaction under deep priors (stay viable, stay socially acceptable), (2) model improvement (learn compressed causal structure and skills), and (3) option preservation (maintain autonomy, resources, and controllable degrees of freedom), with different terms dominating depending on deprivation, uncertainty, and available affordances. A computational study illustrates an alternative action–state objective (Figure) 4. The study also compares empowerment and expected-free-energy agents (Figure).
